---
title: "Three Kinds of Machine"
---

::: {.quest-dialog}
**Prerequisites:** Name the Fears. **Objective:** tell apart a deterministic program, a trained model, and an LLM, and pick the right one.
**Time:** about 10 minutes. <span class="ao-badge">General practice, not a vendor claim.</span>
:::

## Three kinds

- **A deterministic program** (a script, `awk`, `samtools`): the same input always gives the same output, and you can read why. Use it whenever the rule is known.
- **A trained model** (a classifier, a gene-finder, a structure predictor): learned from data to do **one task**, with measured accuracy on that task. Use it when the rule is unknown but the task is narrow and validated.
- **A large language model (LLM)**: trained on large amounts of text, then tuned to follow instructions. Flexible and fluent, with no built-in guarantee of correctness. Use it where the task is open-ended and you can check the result, such as drafting, explaining, or writing a first version of code that you then test.

Two common mistakes: using an LLM to do something a one-line script does exactly (slow, costly, and sometimes wrong), and trusting a model outside the task it was validated for.

An LLM can also be called **inside a script** (for example to tidy free-text labels). That makes your pipeline non-deterministic, so the result needs its own checks and the exact model and version recorded.

## What a model can do on its own

It helps to remember what a language model does well with no tools at all. Apple's developer guide for its small on-device model lists this plainly, and the list is a good reminder for any model on its own (the guide is about a small model, so a large hosted model will do better on some rows):

| A model on its own tends to suit | A model on its own tends to struggle with |
|---|---|
| Summarising and editing text | Counting letters or doing basic arithmetic |
| Pulling out names, places and other entities | Writing code (for that model) |
| Classifying or judging a piece of text | Multi-step logical reasoning |
| Generating tags, or short creative writing | Facts it was never given |

Apple's page says harder tasks become possible once the model can call tools or produce structured output. That is the idea behind an agent: the model reads and writes, and a harness gives it tools (a shell, a file editor, a script runner) for the parts it finds hard. Counting and arithmetic are good examples of work to hand to a script.

## Lore

*Further reading. Optional.*

- [Building effective agents](https://www.anthropic.com/engineering/building-effective-agents): Anthropic, article. Why read: it separates fixed workflows from agents and argues for the simplest option, which is the choice this quest asks you to make.
- [Understand model capabilities](https://developer.apple.com/documentation/foundationmodels/generating-content-and-performing-tasks-with-foundation-models#Understand-model-capabilities): Apple, docs. Why read: it is a short table of what a small on-device model suits and what it does not, a useful reminder of what a model can do before you give it tools.
- [Define success criteria and build evaluations](https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/test-and-evaluate/develop-tests): Anthropic, docs. Why read: it shows how to turn "it seems fine" into a measurable check, which is how you test an LLM step.
:::
